cleanIntro: The Silent Bandit is a titanium-baffle .308-class can built to come apart: the hub mount threads 1-3/8-24 UN-2A and the end cap 1-3/8-24 OD, both meant for removal, and Wilson ships an end cap tool and a hook spanner to do it. ⚠ It has a real cleaning SCHEDULE — every 50-250 rounds depending on use — which is unusual for a rifle can and is the maker's own figure. It is rated for SEMI-AUTOMATIC fire only.

steps.title: Let it cool completely before anything else
steps.action: A suppressor coming off a rifle is hot enough to burn through skin. Wilson makes cooling step one of removal, not a footnote to it. Clear the host — magazine out, action open, chamber checked — while you wait.
steps.prose: The wait is the step. Everything after it is easier on a cold can.
steps.quote: Allow the suppressor to cool completely before attempting removal. Suppressors become extremely hot during use and can cause burns if handled prematurely.
steps.cite: SILENT BANDIT SUPPRESSORS — OWNER’S MANUAL — UNKNOWN — no revision code printed — Step Three: Removal of Suppressor, item 1, p.17
steps.warn: The Suppressor may become extremely hot after use. Never touch a hot suppressor as it can result in injury.

steps.title: Off the barrel counter-clockwise — 1 1/4 inch wrench if it fights
steps.action: Rotate the suppressor counter-clockwise until it is fully unthreaded from the barrel. If it will not start by hand, a 1 1/4 inch open-end wrench is the tool Wilson names.
steps.prose: Reach for the named wrench rather than the adjustable one in the drawer — the flats are sized for it.
steps.quote: A 1 ¼” open end wrench can be used to loosen the suppressor from the barrel if necessary.
steps.cite: SILENT BANDIT SUPPRESSORS — OWNER’S MANUAL — UNKNOWN — no revision code printed — Step Three: Removal of Suppressor, item 3, p.17

steps.title: Apart with the end cap tool and the hub-mount wrench
steps.action: Use the provided end cap tool — it takes a male 1/2 inch square socket — and the provided blast chamber / hub mount wrench to disassemble the suppressor. That is the whole tool list, and both tools ship in the box.
steps.prose: This is a can designed to be opened. The tools are not accessories; they are the procedure.
steps.quote: Use the provided end cap tool (works with male 1/2” square socket) and provided blast chamber / hub mount wrench to disassemble the suppressor.
steps.cite: SILENT BANDIT SUPPRESSORS — OWNER’S MANUAL — UNKNOWN — no revision code printed — Cleaning & Maintenance — Cleaning Procedure, item 1, p.19

steps.title: Every 50-250 rounds — the maker's own interval
steps.action: Wilson publishes a real interval for this can: clean it every 50 to 250 rounds depending on how it is being used and what is going through it. ⚠ For a high-volume shooter that is a range-day job, not an annual one.
steps.prose: Most rifle cans get "as needed". This one gets a number, so use the number.
steps.quote: For optimal performance, clean the suppressor every 50-250 rounds, depending on usage conditions and ammunition type.
steps.cite: SILENT BANDIT SUPPRESSORS — OWNER’S MANUAL — UNKNOWN — no revision code printed — Cleaning & Maintenance — Recommended Cleaning Intervals, p.19

steps.title: Soak the titanium baffle stack, then nylon or brass
steps.action: Soak the titanium baffle stack in a NON-CORROSIVE solvent to loosen the carbon — Wilson names its own Ultima Lube II Carbon Remover. Then scrub the internal components with a nylon or brass brush to take the fouling off.
steps.prose: Non-corrosive is the operative word on titanium. The brush choice matters for the same reason.
steps.quote: Soak the titanium baffle stack in a non-corrosive solvent such as Wilson Combat Ultima Lube II Carbon Remover (part #603-4) to loosen carbon buildup.
steps.cite: SILENT BANDIT SUPPRESSORS — OWNER’S MANUAL — UNKNOWN — no revision code printed — Cleaning & Maintenance — Cleaning Procedure, item 2, p.19
steps.warn: Avoid using harsh chemicals that could degrade the Black Nitride finish or titanium material.

steps.title: Rinse, DRY COMPLETELY, then inspect every part
steps.action: Rinse the components thoroughly with carbon remover and let them dry COMPLETELY before reassembly. Then inspect every part for wear or damage and replace anything compromised — that inspection is a numbered step in Wilson's own procedure, not advice.
steps.prose: A baffle stack reassembled wet traps solvent between the baffles, where nothing will ever get it out.
steps.aside: Inspect all parts for wear or damage and replace any compromised components.
steps.quote: Rinse components thoroughly with carbon remover and allow them to dry completely before reassembly.
steps.cite: SILENT BANDIT SUPPRESSORS — OWNER’S MANUAL — UNKNOWN — no revision code printed — Cleaning & Maintenance — Cleaning Procedure, item 4, p.19

steps.title: Threads clean, lubricated, and anti-seize re-applied
steps.action: Before anything threads together, get all threads and taper surfaces clean and free of debris, and apply the recommended lubricant or grease to stop galling. ⚠ Wilson uses Loctite C5-A anti-seize at manufacture and asks you to re-apply it when the suppressor is reinstalled.
steps.prose: Residue on these surfaces is not cosmetic — Wilson names baffle strikes as the outcome.
steps.quote: Before attaching the suppressor, ensure that all threads and taper surfaces are clean and free from debris. Any residue on these surfaces can result in improper alignment, leading to baffle strikes or damage to the suppressor and firearm.
steps.cite: SILENT BANDIT SUPPRESSORS — OWNER’S MANUAL — UNKNOWN — no revision code printed — Cleaning & Thread Preparation, p.15

steps.title: Hub mount seated with the hook spanner, then the can hand tight
steps.action: Align the suppressor with the hub mount threads and rotate clockwise until it seats firmly against the shoulder, using the included hook spanner wrench for torque. Then thread the suppressor assembly onto the K-Mount adapter HAND TIGHT and inspect visually for alignment with the bore.
steps.prose: Two joints, two different tightnesses. The hub takes a wrench; the can does not.
steps.quote: Suppressor Installation: Thread suppressor assembly onto K-Mount adapter hand tighten. Once the suppressor is threaded onto the adapter, visually inspect for proper alignment with the bore.
steps.cite: SILENT BANDIT SUPPRESSORS — OWNER’S MANUAL — UNKNOWN — no revision code printed — Step Two: Assembling the Suppressor, item 2, p.16

deepSteps.title: K-Mount onto the barrel — 30-50 ft-lb, and stop if it fights
deepSteps.action: Check the Quell K-Mount threads match your barrel's pitch, clean and lightly lubricate them, align slowly and thread it on by hand; Wilson's figure is approximately 30-50 ft-lbs. ⛔ If there is resistance or the hub will not thread smoothly, STOP immediately and call Wilson Combat — do not force it.
deepSteps.prose: Cross-threading a 1-3/8 hub is a barrel repair, not a suppressor repair.
deepSteps.aside: Barrel Torque: 30 ft-lbs is recommended when installing suppressor mounts or muzzle devices.
deepSteps.quote: Take care not to cross-thread or force the suppressor HUB onto the barrel. If resistance occurs or the suppressor HUB does not smoothly thread onto the firearm, stop immediately and contact Wilson Combat Customer Service for guidance
deepSteps.cite: SILENT BANDIT SUPPRESSORS — OWNER’S MANUAL — UNKNOWN — no revision code printed — Step One: Preparation for Installation, p.15

deepSteps.title: ⚠ SEMI-AUTOMATIC RATED — sustained high rates of fire damage it
deepSteps.action: The Silent Bandit is rated for semi-automatic fire. Extended periods at a high rate of fire build heat that may damage the suppressor. That is a usage limit, and exceeding it is a maintenance question you cannot clean your way out of.
deepSteps.prose: Heat damage does not look like fouling and does not come off in a solvent bath.
deepSteps.quote: Rate of Fire: The Silent Bandit is rated for semi-automatic fire. Extended periods at a high rate of fire can produce excessive heat buildup, which may damage the suppressor.
deepSteps.cite: SILENT BANDIT SUPPRESSORS — OWNER’S MANUAL — UNKNOWN — no revision code printed — Usage & Safety Guidelines — Barrel Torque and Rate of Fire, p.18

deepSteps.title: A loose can gets re-seated cold, not re-torqued hot
deepSteps.action: If the suppressor works loose in use, Wilson's answer is to let it cool and then hand-tighten it back firmly against the barrel shoulder. ⛔ And if a baffle strike happens, stop using it immediately and contact Wilson for inspection or repair — that one is not a field fix.
deepSteps.prose: Two troubleshooting entries, two very different severities. Know which one you are looking at.
deepSteps.quote: Allow the suppressor to cool, retighten the suppressor by hand to ensure it is firmly seated against the barrel shoulder.
deepSteps.cite: SILENT BANDIT SUPPRESSORS — OWNER’S MANUAL — UNKNOWN — no revision code printed — Troubleshooting — Loose Suppressor, p.21

deepSteps.title: Thread protectors on the barrel whenever the can is off
deepSteps.action: When the suppressor is not fitted, put a thread protector or a suitable muzzle device on the barrel to protect the threads and the crown in storage and transport. The hook spanner has a storage slot for whichever end cap is not in use.
deepSteps.prose: A dinged crown is a permanent accuracy problem and it happens in a case, not on a range.
deepSteps.quote: Thread Protection: Use thread protectors when the suppressor is not in use to safeguard the barrel threads from damage.
deepSteps.cite: SILENT BANDIT SUPPRESSORS — OWNER’S MANUAL — UNKNOWN — no revision code printed — Recommended Tips for Maintenance & Storage, item 1, p.20

cleaning.name: INTERVAL
tasks: Every 50-250 rounds depending on use and ammunition — Wilson's own figure

cleaning.name: DISASSEMBLY AND SOAK
tasks: End cap tool (male 1/2 inch square socket) plus the hub mount / hook spanner
Titanium baffle stack soaked in a NON-CORROSIVE carbon remover
Nylon or brass brush on the internals
⛔ No harsh chemicals — they degrade Black Nitride and titanium

cleaning.name: RINSE, DRY, INSPECT
tasks: Every part inspected for wear or damage; compromised parts replaced

cleaning.name: THREADS
tasks: All threads and taper surfaces clean and free of debris
Loctite C5-A anti-seize (or equivalent) re-applied on reinstall
Anti-seize on the end cap and HUB mount adaptor threads at all times
Thread protector on the barrel whenever the can is off

reassembly: Threads and tapers clean; anti-seize/grease re-applied.
Hub mount rotated clockwise onto the suppressor until it seats on the shoulder, hook spanner for torque.
Suppressor threaded onto the K-Mount adapter HAND TIGHT.
Visually inspected for alignment with the bore.
Firmly seated, no gaps and no looseness before firing.
fncheck: After installation, confirm the suppressor is firmly seated with no gaps and no looseness — Wilson names misalignment and gaps as the cause of reduced performance, baffle strikes and end cap damage. Verify visually that it is aligned with the bore. ⚠ Then keep checking during use: Wilson's own note is that it is crucial to verify the suppressor remains securely tightened while shooting. Semi-automatic rates only.
